chapter_3_pool.question: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), what is the complete definition of health?
options: A) Merely the absolute absence of any infectious disease or physical injury
B) A state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease
C) Having strong relationships with peer groups and working efficiently without getting tired
D) Following a strict daily routine and eating fresh food suited to one's body constitution

chapter_3_pool.question: According to the traditional Indian system of Ayurveda, what does true health represent?
options: A) Taking antibiotics regularly under a doctor's strict prescription
B) Eradicating all pathogens from the local neighborhood environment
C) A perfect balance of body, mind, and surroundings
D) Performing daily modern functional training exercises without rest

chapter_3_pool.question: What terms are used in Ayurveda to describe the required daily routine and seasonal routine to maintain overall balance?
What does the Ayurvedic term 'prakriti' refer to when selecting a fresh and wholesome diet?
options: A) An individual's unique body constitution
B) The current season of the year
C) The environmental air quality index

chapter_3_pool.question: What parameter is utilized in cities to monitor and communicate how clean or polluted the environmental air is?
When a person feels unwell, what term describes the internal sensations felt by the individual, such as pain or tiredness?
Which of the following is classified as a 'sign' of a disease because it can be objectively seen or measured by a doctor?
What is the general biological term used for disease-causing organisms like bacteria, viruses, fungi, worms, and protozoa?
What name is given to diseases that are not caused by pathogens and do not spread from one individual to another?
Diseases like cancer, diabetes, and asthma that persist for a long time (typically more than 3 months) are referred to as:
Why are non-communicable diseases (NCDs) like diabetes and heart problems becoming significantly more common in India today?
options: A) Because of a sudden increase in airborne viral pathogens across cities
B) Because of lifestyle changes, such as eating more processed food and getting less exercise
C) Because people are neglecting basic handwashing with soap and water
D) Because of contaminated drinking water supplies in major urban centers

chapter_3_pool.question: What term defines insects like mosquitos and houseflies that carry and spread pathogens from an infected person to a healthy person?
According to the bulletin board, how much percent of people in India are currently obese?
According to the textbook, which aquatic plant is responsible for making more than 50% of the oxygen in the atmosphere?
Regular handwashing with soap and clean water is documented to reduce the risk of infection by how much?
An increase in screen time and excessive screen watching in children is directly linked to which specific eye condition?
Which of the following is an airborne communicable disease caused specifically by a virus?
Which organ of the human body serves as the primary site of infection for the disease Tuberculosis (TB)?
What type of causal agent is responsible for the intestinal infection known as Typhoid?
Which communicable disease targets the liver, causing symptoms like nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and jaundice?
The intestinal disease Ascariasis is caused by which category of infectious organisms?
What type of pathogen is responsible for causing Malaria, which is transmitted to humans via mosquito bites?
What alternative name is commonly given to Dengue fever due to the severe muscle and joint pain it inflicts on patients?
Organisms that live inside or on another living being and feed directly on their nutrients are defined as:
What term refers to the natural, inherent ability of our human body to resist and fight off various diseases?
What biological mechanism allows a vaccine to protect an individual from serious physical infections?
options: A) It immediately cures the disease by directly dissolving the cellular wall of the pathogen
B) It trains the immune system to recognize and attack harmful germs, providing acquired immunity
C) It replaces the damaged organs of the body with fresh, synthetic cell structures
D) It balances the digestive juices and acids inside the stomach to neutralize toxins

chapter_3_pool.question: Which pioneering researcher studied the links between hormones, viruses, and cancer, highlighting the risks of tobacco and pollution?
Who discovered the very first vaccine in the late 1700s after observing that milkmaids infected with cowpox became resistant to smallpox?
What was the name of the traditional Indian method used long before modern vaccines to build immunity against smallpox?
What was the name given to the traditional practitioners who performed the process of variolation in ancient India?
Which deadly global disease was completely eradicated worldwide by 1979 through an intensive mass vaccination campaign?
Which prominent Indian scientist played a foundational role in developing the Rotavirus vaccine to protect young children from severe diarrhoea?
What type of specific medical drug is prescribed by doctors to kill bacteria or stop their growth inside the body?
Why are standard antibiotics completely ineffective when used against viral infections like the common cold, cough, or flu?
options: A) Because viruses grow much faster than modern antibiotics can dissolve
B) Because antibiotics specifically target parts of bacterial cells that are completely different from viruses
C) Because viral infections can only be managed by traditional herbs and mineral oils
D) Because antibiotics require massive amounts of oxygen to target a pathogen effectively

chapter_3_pool.question: Who discovered the first bacterial-fighting antibiotic, Penicillin, in 1928 after observing a green mould contamination in a petri dish?
What critical healthcare threat occurs when bacteria adapt, survive, and multiply despite being treated with a specific antibiotic?
What primary patient error directly contributes to the spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in a community?
options: A) Exercising outdoors in a public park with poor air quality
B) Eating processed fast food items containing high sugar and oil content
C) Practicing daily yoga and meditation without proper clinical guidance
D) Taking antibiotics when they are not required or taking an incomplete dose

chapter_3_pool.question: What can happen to the human body if antibiotics are taken unnecessarily and indiscriminately?
options: A) They will immediately turn into active viral strains inside the lungs
B) They kill beneficial bacteria that protect our body from infections along with the bad ones
C) They permanently stop the production of hormonal juices inside the liver
D) They directly cause structural fractures in the bones of the joints

chapter_3_pool.question: To reduce antibiotic resistance, what is the correct practice for using antibiotic medicines?
options: A) Purchase them directly from a chemist whenever you suffer from a sore throat
B) Use them wisely only when prescribed by a doctor, in the correct dose, and for the right duration
C) Mix them with lukewarm milk or fresh fruit juice to maximize their chemical effect
D) Stop taking them as soon as your physical symptoms disappear to save the dosage

chapter_3_pool.question: Which of the following represents a non-communicable nutritional deficiency disease caused by a lack of vitamin C?
What is the core focus of medical therapies designed for managing chronic, non-communicable diseases?
options: A) Complete physical isolation of the patient to prevent transmission to peers
B) Prescribing heavy doses of broad-spectrum antibiotics to clear out cell pathways
C) Managing symptoms and improving quality of life through medication, lifestyle changes, and rehabilitation
D) Applying red-colored stains over the affected organs to improve visibility

chapter_3_pool.question: When a human body encounters a specific pathogen for the second time, why is the secondary immune response much stronger than the first encounter?
options: A) Because the pathogen becomes weak and fragile over time
B) Because the immune system has been trained to recognize and launch a targeted attack against that specific germ
C) Because the body's internal temperature rises automatically to burn off the pathogens
D) Because antibiotics remain permanently active in the bloodstream for years

chapter_3_pool.question: What clinical practice involves injecting an inactivated bacterial toxin, such as a shot given immediately after an injury, to protect against bacterial infections?
What clear lesson was derived from the community-led sanitation campaign in Bhadrak district, Odisha?
options: A) Air pollution can be managed completely by limiting digital screen time
B) Improving sanitation and reducing open defecation significantly lowers cases of diarrhoea and infections
C) Traditional medical herbs are highly effective at completely replacing modern vaccines
D) Mass vaccination campaigns are entirely dependent on urban industrial sectors

chapter_3_pool.question: What basic health mantra is promoted by the national Fit India Movement regarding daily dietary habits?
options: A) Increase the consumption of highly processed and packed meals
B) Completely eliminate protein-rich grains from daily meals
C) Reduce the amount of oil and sugar in the diet
D) Take active bacterial supplements with every breakfast meal
